title: 3 Days in Lisbon: What You Actually Have to See
titleTag: 3 Days in Lisbon: The Must-See Itinerary
ogTitle: 3 Days in Lisbon — The Must-See Itinerary
metaDescription: The essential three-day Lisbon itinerary: the castle, Alfama, Belém and the Baixa hills, grouped by neighbourhood so you climb each one only once.

standfirst: Three days is enough for Lisbon's essentials, but only if you group them properly. Here is what genuinely has to be on the list, in the order that saves you the most walking.
cardSummary: The castle, Alfama, Belém and the Baixa hills — what to see and what to skip.

heroImage.alt: Alfama's terracotta rooftops sloping down to the River Tagus, seen from Miradouro das Portas do Sol
heroImage.caption: Alfama from Miradouro das Portas do Sol — the view most people picture when they picture Lisbon.
heroImage.workTitle: Alfama from Miradouro das Portas do Sol, Lisbon

body: Three days covers Lisbon's essentials comfortably: the castle and Alfama, the monuments at Belém, and the Baixa and Chiado hills in the middle. What it does not cover is Sintra, which needs a full day of its own and is the thing most three-day itineraries wrongly try to squeeze in.
The plan below groups everything by neighbourhood. Lisbon is built on hills, and the difference between a well-ordered day and a badly ordered one is roughly two hours of unnecessary climbing.
**The maps lie about the hills.** A 700 m walk between two viewpoints can be a ten-minute climb on cobbles. Distances here are short; the gradients are not.

sections.heading: Day 1 — The castle and Alfama
body: Start high and walk down. São Jorge Castle sits at the top of the city's oldest hill, and every other stop on this day is below it — so doing the climb once, first thing, is the whole trick.
Alfama is the medieval quarter that survived the 1755 earthquake, and it is the one part of Lisbon best seen without a plan. Get deliberately lost in it.

sections.alt: The stone walls and towers of São Jorge Castle on the hill above Lisbon
sections.caption: São Jorge Castle. The walls, not the interior, are what you came for.

sections.heading: The must-sees
sections.note: All within walking distance of each other, arranged downhill.

stops.name: São Jorge Castle
stops.detail: Ramparts with a full sweep over the city and the river. Quietest in the first hour after opening.

stops.name: Miradouro das Portas do Sol
stops.detail: The classic Alfama view, straight down over the rooftops to the water. A few minutes' walk below the castle.

stops.name: Alfama's lanes
stops.detail: The oldest quarter in the city. No route required — head downhill and let the streets do the work.

stops.name: Lisbon Cathedral (Sé)
stops.detail: The city's oldest building, fortress-like, at the bottom of the hill. A quick stop rather than a long one.

stops.name: Fado in Alfama
stops.detail: The small fado houses are the real thing and they fill up. Book ahead rather than turning up.

sections.heading: Day 2 — Belém
body: Belém is 6 km west of the centre and holds most of Lisbon's heavyweight monuments in a single riverside strip. It is a half day of sights and a full day if you take it slowly.
Go early. Both major monuments have timed entry and both sell out. The train from Cais do Sodré takes about ten minutes; the riverside tram is slower and prettier, which makes it the better way back.

sections.alt: The long limestone facade of Jerónimos Monastery in Belém, Lisbon
sections.caption: Jerónimos Monastery. The cloister is the reason to come — not the church, which is free and far busier.

sections.heading: The must-sees
sections.note: Book Jerónimos before you travel. It has the worst walk-up queue in the city.

stops.name: Jerónimos Monastery
stops.detail: The high point of Manueline architecture and the single most impressive building in Lisbon. Pay for the cloister.

stops.name: Pastéis de Belém
stops.detail: The original custard tart bakery, next door. The takeaway counter queue moves much faster than it looks.

stops.name: Padrão dos Descobrimentos
stops.detail: The Discoveries monument on the waterfront, with a lift to a viewing deck over the river.

stops.name: Belém Tower
stops.detail: Twenty flat minutes further along the river. Worth seeing from the outside even if the queue puts you off going in.

sections.alt: Belém Tower, a white limestone fortified tower standing in the River Tagus
sections.caption: Belém Tower, built to guard the harbour and now standing at the edge of the river.

sections.heading: Day 3 — Baixa, Chiado and the viewpoints
body: The centre is the flattest part of the city and the hills on either side are the steepest. This day alternates between them, which is easier than it sounds if you use the funiculars.
If you want to ride Tram 28, do it at opening or late in the evening. In the middle of the day it is a long queue for a crowded ride.

sections.heading: The must-sees
sections.note: The flat grid first, then one climb, then sunset.

stops.name: Praça do Comércio
stops.detail: The great riverfront square, and the obvious place to start. Walk north through the Baixa grid from here.

stops.name: Santa Justa Lift
stops.detail: A wrought-iron lift connecting the lower town to Chiado. The queue is long; the walk around it takes five minutes.

stops.name: Carmo Convent
stops.detail: A gothic church left roofless by the 1755 earthquake and never rebuilt. The most atmospheric ruin in the city.

stops.name: Time Out Market
stops.detail: Thirty-odd stalls from well-known Lisbon kitchens under one roof. Busy, but genuinely good.

stops.name: Miradouro da Senhora do Monte
stops.detail: The highest viewpoint in Lisbon and the least crowded of the famous ones. The best sunset in the city.

sections.heading: What three days does not cover
sections.intro: Cutting deliberately beats rushing. These need more time than you have:
items: **Sintra** — a full day, not a half day. Rushing it is worse than saving it for a longer trip.
**Cascais** — pleasant, and entirely optional on a first visit.
**The big museums** (Gulbenkian, Ancient Art) — excellent, and a half day each.
**A second viewpoint circuit** — after three miradouros they begin to blur.

faqHeading: Common questions about 3 days in Lisbon

faq.a: For the city itself, yes. Three days covers the castle, Alfama, Belém and the Baixa and Chiado hills at a reasonable pace. It is not enough to add Sintra properly, which needs a full day of its own.

faq.q: What are the must-see attractions in Lisbon?
faq.a: São Jorge Castle, the Alfama district, Jerónimos Monastery and Belém Tower are the four nobody should miss. After those, the Carmo Convent ruins and a sunset from Miradouro da Senhora do Monte are the strongest additions.
Only in the first hour of service or late in the evening. In the middle of the day it is a long queue for a crowded ride, and walking the same route through Graça and Alfama shows you more of it.

faq.q: Do I need to book Jerónimos Monastery in advance?
faq.a: Yes. It is the busiest ticketed sight in Lisbon and the walk-up queue is long for most of the year. Book a timed slot before you travel and arrive near opening.

Very, but it is steep. The distances are short and the hills are not. Budget roughly double the time your map suggests for anything between the river and the castle, and use the funiculars and metro when your legs have had enough.
